rows: The Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 establish the principal HSE-enforced workplace requirements for ionising radiation.
Employers working with ionising radiation must assess risk and apply controls proportionate to the radiation-protection risk.
Regulatory control uses notification, registration or consent depending on the level and type of work.
Employers may need radiation-protection advisers and radiation-protection supervisors to support compliance.
The annual dose limit for occupational exposure to the lens of the eye is 20 mSv under the updated regime.
Procedures are required to estimate doses to members of the public where relevant.
Employees must cooperate with employers in meeting ionising-radiation requirements.
Specified ionising-radiation work can require statutory medical surveillance by an HSE-appointed doctor.
A mapped site or building use does not establish radiation dose, source activity or regulatory-control tier.
Applicability depends on the source, activity, dose assessment, work practice, exemptions and authorisation status.
REPPIR 2019 guidance supports operators and local authorities in preparing for and responding to radiation emergencies.
The regulations concern work with ionising radiation, with their full requirements applying mainly to licensed nuclear sites.
Emergency planning should be proportionate to the assessed radiation-emergency risk.
Operators and local authorities have distinct preparedness and response responsibilities.
Public-information arrangements form part of radiation-emergency preparedness.
Preparedness includes arrangements for foreseeable radiation emergencies and coordinated response.
REPPIR is part of the legal framework relevant to ionising-radiation work.
The approved code provides practical guidance for meeting regulatory duties.
General emergency-planning guidance does not demonstrate that a specific parcel lies within an emergency-planning zone.
Local conclusions require current operator assessments, regulatory designations and authorised emergency-planning data.
Private landlords must keep rented homes safe and free from health hazards.
Gas equipment supplied by a landlord must be safely installed and maintained by a Gas Safe registered engineer.
Relevant gas appliances and flues require annual safety checks and the tenant must receive the safety record.
Landlords must ensure the electrical system and supplied appliances are safe.
Landlords must provide required smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms.
Tenants must have access to escape routes and supplied furnishings must meet fire-safety requirements.
Large houses in multiple occupation can require additional fire alarms and extinguishers.
Alarm guidance describes responsibilities to repair or replace faulty alarms after the landlord is informed.
Published landlord duties do not prove the current condition or compliance of a specific rented property.
Requirements depend on tenure, appliance type, HMO status, occupancy and current inspection evidence.
Relevant landlords must provide at least one smoke alarm on each storey containing living accommodation.
A carbon-monoxide alarm is required in rooms used as living accommodation containing a fixed combustion appliance, excluding gas cookers.
Landlords must repair or replace a required alarm once informed and after finding that it is faulty.
The amended requirements apply to relevant social and private rented homes in England.
Local housing authorities enforce the alarm requirements.
Authorities can serve remedial notices where they have reasonable grounds to believe a landlord is non-compliant.
If a landlord fails to comply with a remedial notice, the authority can arrange remedial action subject to occupier consent.
The landlord and tenant guidance is non-statutory and is not a substitute for the regulations.
An alarm requirement does not prove that an installed alarm is present, powered, correctly located or functioning.
Property-level conclusions require inspection, tenancy and appliance evidence rather than tenure classification alone.
